Consult Summary:
- 23-year-old woman with 2 days of constant dull suprapubic/lower abdominal ache with nausea, subjective feverishness (hot/sweaty), increased urinary frequency and recent pink-tinged urine/spotting; clinician recommended same-day face-to-face review and pregnancy testing to exclude pregnancy/ectopic.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Two days of a constant dull ache below the umbilicus (suprapubic), associated with nausea and feeling hot/sweaty.
  - Reports increased urinary frequency.
  - Noted pink-tinged urine or spotting for the last couple of days; expecting her period soon (last menstrual period ~3+ weeks ago).
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began ~2 days ago, gradual onset, constant since onset.
  - History of constipation ~1 week ago which has resolved; had a normal bowel motion yesterday.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - No clear exacerbating or relieving factors reported.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Nausea present; no vomiting.
  - Increased urinary frequency without dysuria, urgency, or malodour.
  - No vaginal discharge.
  - Denies light-headedness or syncope.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No vomiting, no painful urination/stinging, no urinary urgency, no vaginal discharge, no severe unilateral pelvic pain, no measured fever recorded.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Surgical history: not mentioned.
- Notable family history: brother with type 1 diabetes.

Medications:
- Contraception: Implanon (etonogestrel) implant — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other regular medications reported.

Allergies:
- Amoxicillin (patient-reported).

Social History:
- Lives with boyfriend; sexually active with a single regular partner.
- Non-smoker.
- No alcohol/substance use history documented.

Family History:
- Brother: type 1 diabetes.
- No other relevant family history reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (clinician recommended face-to-face examination).

Investigations:
- None performed during this consult.
- Clinician advised: pregnancy test and face-to-face assessment; further tests (e.g., urine testing, pelvic exam, imaging) to be done in person.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Acute suprapubic/lower abdominal pain with nausea and intermenstrual spotting in a patient with an etonogestrel implant — pregnancy (including threatened miscarriage or ectopic) must be excluded urgently; differential includes urinary tract infection (possible haematuria), pelvic inflammatory disease, and post-constipation/functional bowel pain.

DDx Integration (top items aligned with transcript):
1) Pregnancy-related pathology (threatened miscarriage or ectopic) — Supporting: recent spotting/pink urine, lower abdominal pain, sexually active; Opposing: Implanon in situ (low pregnancy risk). Clinician specifically advised ruling out pregnancy.  
2) Urinary tract infection / acute cystitis with possible haematuria — Supporting: increased urinary frequency, suprapubic ache, pink-tinged urine; Opposing: no dysuria/urgency and no urine testing yet.  
3) Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or adnexal pathology — Supporting: lower abdominal pain and intermenstrual spotting, sexually active; Opposing: no vaginal discharge, single partner, relatively mild/dull pain.

Issue 1: Possible pregnancy-related pathology (including threatened miscarriage / ectopic)
- Assessment:
  - Must be excluded given spotting and abdominal pain despite contraceptive implant.
- Plan:
  - Urgent urine pregnancy test (urine β-hCG) at face-to-face appointment today (clinician recommended).
  - If pregnancy test positive: arrange prompt clinical review and consider urgent transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to exclude ectopic pregnancy; refer to emergency services/ED if severe pain, haemodynamic compromise, syncope, or heavy bleeding.
  - If pregnancy test negative but symptoms persist/worsen, consider repeat testing per local protocol and further assessment.
  - Safety netting: patient instructed to seek urgent care if worsening pain, light-headedness, fainting, or heavy vaginal bleeding.

Issue 2: Possible urinary tract infection / haematuria
- Assessment:
  - Clinical features (suprapubic ache, increased frequency, pink urine) compatible with cystitis/haematuria but absence of dysuria/urgency makes classic presentation less certain.
- Plan:
  - Urine dipstick and midstream urine (MSU) sample for microscopy/culture at face-to-face appointment.
  - If urine testing indicates infection or if clinical exam supports UTI, consider appropriate antibiotic therapy guided by allergy (amoxicillin allergy noted) and local guidelines — prescribe after in-person assessment and test results.
  - Provide symptomatic advice pending review; arrange follow-up for culture results and reassessment.

Issue 3: PID / adnexal pathology vs post-constipation / functional bowel pain
- Assessment:
  - PID possible given pain and intermenstrual bleeding, though absence of discharge and lower risk sexual history reduce probability; adnexal pathology (ovarian cyst/rupture/torsion) less likely given subacute dull pain but cannot be excluded without exam/imaging. Recent constipation could explain some suprapubic discomfort but constipation reportedly resolved.
- Plan:
  - Face-to-face pelvic examination (including speculum and bimanual exam) and, if indicated, STI testing (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT) as part of in-person assessment.
  - Consider pelvic ultrasound if exam findings suggest adnexal mass, focal unilateral severe pain, or if pregnancy test positive and ectopic must be excluded.
  - If PID diagnosed clinically, consider empiric antibiotic therapy per guidelines taking into account amoxicillin allergy (choice to be made after in-person evaluation).
  - If symptoms are consistent with post-constipation bowel pain and no other cause identified, manage conservatively and arrange follow-up.

General plan items:
- Patient agreed to attend same-day face-to-face GP review today for physical exam and investigations.
- Immediate tests recommended at face-to-face visit: urine pregnancy test (urine β-hCG), urine dip/MSU, pelvic/speculum/bimanual exam, and STI screening if indicated.
- Escalation/safety netting: return to ED or contact clinician urgently for worsening pain, syncope/light-headedness, severe bleeding, or any new concerning symptoms.
- Note allergy to amoxicillin when selecting antibiotics.

Quality checks:
- Missing/expected elements: no vitals recorded; no physical examination findings available; no urine pregnancy test, urine dip, MSU, STI tests, or imaging documented — these were recommended but not yet performed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none significant; DDx recommendations (pregnancy test, consider UTI, PID) are consistent with clinician comments in transcript.
- Transcript quality: clear conversation with minimal inaudible content; clinician recommended face-to-face assessment and tests.
